name: PT Golden Energy Mines Tbk

frontmatter.title: Golden Energy Mines — a low-cost contract-of-work thermal producer priced on the cycle, with a konglo-regime overlay on the target
frontmatter.summary: GEMS is a low-cost contractor-operated Indonesian thermal coal miner controlled by PT Dian Swastatika Sentosa in the Widjaja family's Sinar Mas group. We hold HOLD: the finite-life through-cycle DCF sits below the market price, the konglo lens keeps part of the premium, and the thin return rests on an undeclared, unguided FY2026 final dividend. The HSC exclusion is operative from 2 November, confirming the lens's flag and changing no fundamental input.
thesis: Through-cycle value, not spot earnings, anchors the call: our finite-life reserve DCF, priced off the house coal deck long-run Newcastle marker and the FY2025A realised ratio, now stops at the two sourced CCoW terms rather than at the last reserve tonne, so it sits below the market price and the expected return is thin and dividend-carried rather than re-rating-led.

The konglo-regime overlay is a target adjustment, not a valuation input: the price is a premium to fundamental value today, and the lens keeps only part of it over the twelve-month regime scenarios because GEMS sits on the HSC list — formally out of the IHSG calculation from 2 November 2026 — and faces a free-float step due inside the window, an overlay that lifts the target toward the price without touching the fundamental work.

The royalty is charged the way the LK shows it being paid: GEMS mines under contract-of-work licences whose share-of-production royalty the contract states, so we charge that contract rate flat — not the IUPK succession schedule for ex-contract holders, a licence class GEMS does not hold.

The realised-price discount is the largest single swing both ways: we calibrate the realised-to-benchmark ratio on the FY2025A actual and hold it flat, so the DCF does not inherit the FY2026E benchmark spike.

The reserve base is finite and licensed: the DCF values only the tonnes inside BORNEO's and BSL's sourced CCoW terms, and the blocks outside them — WRL's booked reserve and the TBBU/KIM development tonnes — are carried in the bridge at their sourced sunk book value, not at zero and not at a DCF value no licence or plan supports; the DCF has no perpetuity tail and carries no mine-closure charge, which we disclose rather than shock.

The dividend is the market anchor, but we bank only cash that is either paid or can be paid: the FY2026 interim is already paid and deducted in the bridge, the yield cross-check is excluded because it capitalises a peak-year payout, and the final tranche in our return is not declared — the HOLD is a dividend bet with a thin cushion, not a re-rating call.

blocks.text: **What changed in this update.** The exchange's high-shareholding-concentration (HSC) exclusion has become operative: from Monday 2 November 2026 the HSC shares — GEMS among them — are out of the IHSG calculation and out of the LQ45, IDX30 and IDX80, while they continue to trade normally and are not delisted [S15, S16, S18]. This is the step we flagged when the rule was first applied, now dated and in force: it confirms the konglo lens's HSC flag and removes the timing uncertainty around it, but it removes passive index demand only — not a tonne, a licence, a cash flow or a dividend [S15, S16]. We therefore change no fundamental input, no scenario probability, no weight and no rating; the target, the fundamental value and the return below are the engine's current output at today's FX and price. The only input that has moved since the published version is the rupiah exchange rate, which shifts the rupiah figures by a rounding amount; nothing in the business case or the regime reading has changed. The prior revision's two changes stand unchanged: the DCF is still cut at the group's two sourced CCoW production terms, and the FY2026 interim paid on 22 October 2026 is still deducted once in the bridge and excluded from the forward dividend [S3, S7]. Separately, OJK has said it is considering a criminal path in its DSSA/BREN/CUAN market-manipulation case [S17]; no GEMS entity is named, and we keep this subsidiary's own view independent of the parent-level development, treating it only as a governance watch item [S17].

We update coverage of PT Golden Energy Mines at **HOLD** with a target of **Rp6,721**, a total return of **5.2%** against the last price of Rp7,150. The call rests on our primary method — a finite-life, through-cycle discounted cash flow of the licensed reserve base — which values the equity at Rp6,879, with our EV/EBITDA cross-check at Rp6,427; the blend (weights 71% and 29%) is rolled forward and set against the market. The dividend-yield cross-check, which screens far above both, stays **excluded** because it capitalises the FY2026E peak payout [S0]. The return carries only the cash still to come: the modelled FY2026 final dividend of **Rp804** a share, added to a target that itself sits below the price. That final tranche is **not declared and not guided** — it is the model residual of the demonstrated payout policy over FY2026 parent profit after the interim, payable only if the board declares it — and it carries nearly the whole total return, so the HOLD, not the target, is the dividend bet: at the low end of the group's own payout record the final tranche would shrink toward nothing and the call would move to REDUCE [S0, S7]. The US$200.0m interim (F13) was paid on 22 October 2026, after the 30 June 2026 balance sheet and before the valuation date, so it is deducted from equity in the bridge and excluded from the forward dividend — counted once, not twice [S0, S7].

This is a konglo name, so the fundamental value and the market price are two different things and the report keeps them apart. Our fundamental twelve-month value is **Rp6,215**, and our value today is Rp6,300; the market's Rp7,150 is 1.13× the value-today figure and a somewhat larger premium to the twelve-month fundamental value, which rolls forward at the cost of equity. Both bases are stated because both are load-bearing. The konglo lens — the engine's regime step, not a valuation input — keeps only part of that premium over the twelve-month horizon: the price is above value, and the regime flags (HSC, a free-float step due inside the window) slow the climb back toward value. The target therefore sits above fundamental value but below the price, and the return is carried by the final dividend rather than by a re-rating [S0, S9, S10].

GEMS is a low-cost, contractor-operated thermal coal miner in the Sinar Mas group, selling a low-calorific Indonesian product into a domestic-heavy book with Chinese and Indian export offtake [S3]. Coal sales of 54.9 Mt (F1) generated revenue of US$2,414.1m in FY2025 (F10) at a realised price of 40.5% of the Newcastle marker; the company targets up to 58.0 Mt of production and sales in 2026 [S6].

Three things move the value. First, the **realised price**: we calibrate the realised-to-benchmark ratio on the FY2025A actual and hold it flat at 40.5%, so the DCF does not inherit the FY2026E benchmark spike of 137.0 USD/t — a ratio fitted to a spike year would carry that spike relationship into the long run. FY2025A is a normal price year, not a trough: the deck's FY2025A marker of 108.4 USD/t sits at its own long-run level, so this flat ratio is a plain input rather than a conservative haircut. The discount reflects the low-CV product and the large domestic offtake; the bull case lifts the ratio a couple of points as higher-value offtake improves the mix while the bear carries a lower ratio as the new normal — the same driver, mirrored. Second, the **royalty**: GEMS mines under contract-of-work licences whose share-of-production royalty the LK states as 13.5% of coal produced (F9), and we charge that contract rate flat at 12.9% of revenue because the IUPK succession schedule is a licence class GEMS does not hold [S3]. Third, the **reserve life and licence terms**: of the disclosed 844.4 Mt (F3), we value only the tonnes inside BORNEO's 527.0 Mt (F48) and BSL's 183.8 Mt (F49) CCoW blocks, whose production terms run to about 2036 and 2041 respectively (F38, F46); the DCF therefore stops at FY2037E — a finite-life value with no terminal tail, and no mine-closure charge, which we disclose rather than shock. The blocks outside the two CCoW terms are not valued at zero: WRL carries US$0.4m of booked exploration-and-evaluation asset against 2,027 tonnes of booked reserve — its IUP runs only to 19 November 2027 (F50) and the block produced no tonnes in the LK's own table — and the TBBU/KIM development block carries US$1.6m of mine property against its booked tonnes. Both enter the bridge at those sourced sunk-cost floors, per the house rule that a development project is never carried at zero; the extension and development upside they represent is disclosed, not capitalised [S3].

Coal miners in Indonesia are usually valued on the worth of the tonnes in the ground at a normalised
price, not on one year's earnings, because earnings swing with the seaborne price while the resource
does not. A low-cost producer keeps a margin through a trough that a high-cost producer loses, so
cost position — not the spot price — separates a survivor from a name that needs a permanently high
price to justify its value.

GEMS mines and trades thermal coal through Indonesian subsidiaries. It reports two segments — coal mining and coal trading — plus a small "others" leg, and mining is effectively the whole business: the trading segment's revenue and cost of revenue near-offset, leaving the mining leg to carry group profit [S3]. Export sales run mainly to China and India, while domestic sales are the majority of revenue, with China the largest single destination country [S3]; the group is looking to add destinations beyond its core China-India book [S6], which matters because the export leg carries the price upside while the domestic leg is capped, so mix moves realised price without moving volume.

The product is a lower-calorific Indonesian thermal coal: the realised price in FY2025 stood at 40.5% of the Newcastle marker, a discount reflecting quality and the large domestic offtake [S0, S3]. The company has not disclosed a strip ratio, so our intensity factor is an assumption tied to the group's wider coal book, but the cost reality shows in the margin: the contractor-operated model runs a small capital-expenditure line (US$19.2m, F11) and a working-capital cycle dominated by receivables and payables rather than inventory [S0, S3].

The group is acquisitive — several licence holders in the reserve statement entered through business combinations — and goodwill is tested annually for impairment, with charges taken on weaker cash-generating units [S3]. It runs a portfolio of concessions across Kalimantan and Sumatra through subsidiary licence holders, and the reserve statement lists the blocks individually and reconciles them to one group total (F3, F4), so the assets are managed as one book rather than discrete mines [S3]. The strategy is volume-led and cost-led rather than price-led: because the product is a commodity, the management lever is tonnes and cost per tonne, and the group buys scale through adjacent licences and a trading leg that moves third-party coal [S3]. GEMS is a subsidiary of PT Dian Swastatika Sentosa (DSSA) inside the Sinar Mas group, and is the vehicle through which most of the group's listed coal volume flows [S0, S3].

Seaborne thermal-coal demand is driven by Chinese and Indian power generation, and Indonesia is the largest exporter. An Indonesian producer's realised price does not track Newcastle directly: the discount at which its lower-grade coal clears, and the regulated price for domestic power-station tonnes, open a wide and persistent gap between marker and received price. Our sector deck prices this name against the reviewed Newcastle 6,000 kcal/kg NAR series — the coal series that carries both a fiscal-year actual, so the engine can re-price the last year, and a through-cycle forecast path. The deck's other reviewed Indonesian series is the HBA, but that is the high-GAR (6,322 kcal) reference — the wrong grade for GEMS's low-CV product — and the correctly-graded HBA I/II/III carry a spot print only, with no forecast path, while the ICI indices are not reachable public prints. So the whole product discount sits in our realisation assumption rather than in a national index, and the name stays consistent with the rest of the coal batch [S3].

Regulation defines the economics. Royalties sit inside cost of revenue: the group's contract-of-work licences carry a fixed share-of-production royalty (F9), and because a coal contract of work keeps its own PNBP terms until the contract term ends, GEMS's royalty does not step with the government reference price the way the newer IUPK succession schedule does — a licence class GEMS does not hold, so the state's take here is a stable share of the selling price rather than a rising band [S3]. The domestic market obligation caps the price on domestic power tonnes, which mutes the domestic leg's upside in a strong market, and mine licences are finite but extendable with reserve consumption reconciled each year (F3, F4) [S3]. We carry the DMO link as an inert input: the power-cap model is set to the domestic power cap of 70.0 USD/t against a realised price below it, so it binds nothing at today's prices; the capped share of volume is an engine-default proxy with no disclosed power-versus-industrial split behind it, so the DMO's bite is tested through the bear volume shock, not the cap [S3].

Competitively, GEMS is a large-volume, low-cost producer: our LK-calibrated cash cost is low on the tonnes the LK discloses, which leaves a margin through the trough. We call it calibrated low cost rather than a first-quartile rank, which would need a named cost-curve source we do not have, so the claim rests on the LK's own cost of revenue and not on a published curve [S3]. Its edge is that cost position plus the group's integrated marketing and logistics reach, not a differentiated product. Buyer power is material (large Chinese and Indian utilities, a regulated domestic buyer); supplier power is low (competing mining contractors); substitution from renewables and gas is a slow structural threat; new entry is gated by RKAB permitting; and rivalry is intense on price but disciplined on volume when the quota binds.

The seaborne thermal market is a zero-sum contest between exporting nations: Indonesian supply, gated by the annual RKAB quota, competes with Australian, Russian and South African tonnes for Chinese and Indian demand that is itself slowing [S6], which is why the deck's long-run Newcastle marker sits well below spot — it reverts toward a level that clears marginal supply without a permanent war premium. For GEMS the question is the price at the margin and how much the state takes before the shareholder sees it.

Market share and moat. GEMS is one of the larger Indonesian producers and a low-cost one by our LK calibration — we rank it on the LK's own cost of revenue rather than against a published cost curve, because the desk has no named cost-curve source, so we call it low-cost on its disclosures and do not assert a quartile [S3]. In a commodity business the moat is cost position and logistics reach, and its durability turns on strip ratio, contractor pricing and proximity to port, none disclosed well enough to underwrite a permanent advantage, so we treat the cost edge as cycle survival rather than a franchise. On the five forces, rivalry is intense and disciplined only when the quota binds, buyer power is the strongest, supplier power is low, entry is administratively gated, and substitution is the slow structural threat already in the deck's falling long-run marker [S3].

External influences. The three that matter are policy (royalty and licence terms, RKAB quotas, the domestic market obligation), the seaborne price (the deck's Newcastle series and the gas-market link that sets the Asian switching band), and the currency (a rupiah cost base against a dollar revenue line) [S3].

The seaborne thermal market has no differentiation beyond quality grades, so producers compete on cost
and logistics. The same terminal price produces very different margins for a low-cost and a high-cost
producer; Indonesian sellers accept a quality discount to the benchmark in exchange for proximity to
Asian buyers, which is why the realised-to-marker ratio — not the marker itself — is the number that
matters for a name like this one.

Half-year check. The FY2026E forecast is not blind to the first-half actuals: the half-year LK [S5] prints first-half revenue of US$1,495.3m on first-half production of 28.7 Mt, so the first-half realised price, the operating-expense ratio (F36) and the cash royalty and deadrent paid (F37) can be read off the filing and set against our full-year forecast [S5]. FY2026E is a peak-earnings year, and because the dividend cross-check that capitalised it is excluded from the target, the peak year no longer prices the call — the DCF values the reserve base through the cycle. The US$200.0m interim (F13) was declared and paid on 22 October 2026 — part of the FY2026 dividend, already out of the equity value and excluded from the forward return in the valuation section [S7, S0].

FY2025 was a volume-up, price-led down year on a normal benchmark — not a trough: revenue of US$2,414.1m (F10) fell year on year while volumes rose to 54.9 Mt (F1), on a deck benchmark (108.4 USD/t) that sits at its own long-run level; cost of revenue was US$1,642.8m, gross profit US$771.2m, and EBITDA US$378.9m at a margin of 15.7% [S0]. Net profit to the parent was US$258.2m [S0]. Our forecast steps volume to the company's 58.0 Mt target in FY2026 (F14) and holds it near that level, with FY2026E revenue of US$3,218.1m and EBITDA of US$814.4m [S0].

The FY2025A EBITDA identity, reconciled. The data pack's FY2025A EBITDA of US$378.9m [S0] adds back only the income-statement depreciation of US$16.5m (F5), while the group's full depreciation *and* amortisation charge is US$37.1m (F16) — the difference is the mine-property depletion carried inside cost of revenue (F20, F21), which the pack's add-back misses. Re-pricing the first forecast year at FY2025A benchmark, volume and cost, the engine's rebuild of the last year lands about a sixteenth above the pack's figure — the calibration gap the qc check reports — and essentially all of that gap is the missing D&A add-back: on the full charge the two agree to within a percent. **The model's side is right, and the pack understates FY2025A EBITDA** by roughly the D&A difference (it adds back only the income-statement line): the engine's re-priced rebuild — the figure the DCF carries into its forecast — adds back the full charge, while the model's FY2025A *reported* EBITDA line stays on the pack's income-statement basis and differs from the rebuild by that same D&A gap, so the two are not literally one basis and we state both rather than smooth the difference away. The EV/EBITDA cross-check applies its peer-and-history multiple — itself struck on the peers' own reported EBITDA — to that reported FY2025A EBITDA, so that method stays on the reported definition while the DCF, the primary, carries the rebuilt figure [S0, S3].

Cash cost discipline and the D&A charge. The desk's cash-cost identity is cost of revenue less royalty less D&A, so the D&A that enters it must be the true charge, and at GEMS the charge is split. The LK's income-statement depreciation was US$16.5m in FY2025 (F5), but the group's own segment note discloses consolidated depreciation *and* amortisation of US$37.1m for the same year (F16), because mine-property depletion and stripping amortisation sit inside cost of revenue rather than in the depreciation line [S3]. **F5 is contained in F16** — the segment total is the income-statement depreciation plus the amortisation lines, so a reader must not add the two. We model D&A on the full charge, US$0.68 per tonne; using the pack's D&A alone would understate the charge and, through the identity, overstate cash cost [S3]. The segment-note path is volatile (US$19.2m in FY2022, US$60.5m in FY2023, US$0.6m in FY2024 and US$37.1m in FY2025), and the FY2024 point is not mis-stated but anomalous — the company's own printed figure, revenue-tied to the FY2024 accounts (F18), yet below even that year's income-statement depreciation (US$12.7m, F6) — so we take the FY2025 full charge (US$37.1m, F16) as the least-distorted recent year and rebuild FY2024 from the notes [S3, S4, S8]. Its sourced components still fall short of the segment total by roughly a tenth, a residual the LK does not itemise; we flag it rather than smooth it, and since the unit cash cost is derived by subtracting D&A from cost of revenues, the base case takes the segment-total end [S3].

Royalty — the contract rate the LK is charged. Our model charges a single, flat royalty: the coal-contract-of-work share-of-production rate the LK discloses. The producing entities mine under Coal Contracts of Work — BORNEO holds CCoW No. 007/PK/PTBA-BI/1994 and BSL holds No. 015/PK/PTBA-BL/1994 — and the LK states the charge plainly: BORNEO must share its coal production with the Government of the Republic of Indonesia (13.5%, F9) [S3]. Because a coal contract of work keeps its own royalty terms until the contract term ends, that rate is a stable share of what GEMS receives rather than a band that rises with the government reference price; the IUPK succession schedule is a different licence class, and the LK's licence note shows GEMS's producing entities holding contract-of-work and IUP licences, not IUPK [S3]. The LK's own royalty line confirms the contract rate is the rate being paid: US$312.4m inside cost of revenues in FY2025 (F7), US$339.8m the prior year (F8) and US$452.2m in FY2023 (F31) — each an effective rate that brackets the 13.5% contract share [S3, S8]. Because the contract share is levied on coal produced valued at the government reference — which reproduced the LK's booked royalty exactly in the last audited year — a production share is not a share of realised revenue, so we charge the FY2025A effective rate of 12.9% of revenue flat across the forecast; our FY2026E royalty of US$415.1m reads 12.9% of that year's revenue [S0, S3]. The read the previous version took — the top IUPK band, charged by assertion — is the alternative **not adopted**: it is a licence-class error rather than a conservative read.

The half-year royalty line reconciles, once the cash and accrual bases are separated. The cash-flow statement shows US$203.4m of royalty fees *and deadrent paid* in the first half (F37), which reads against first-half revenue as a higher percentage than the modelled rate; but the royalty *expense* charged inside cost of revenues for the same half was US$192.1m (F59), the difference being the step-up in advance royalty and a small movement in accrued royalty, while deadrent is a fixed area fee in general and administrative expense rather than a share of production. On the expense basis the first-half charge is in line with the modelled contract rate, so we do not raise the rate on a cash-timing artefact [S5, S3]. Realisation remains the larger swing than royalty, as the sensitivity table shows.

Closure and rehabilitation. The reserve base is finite and the DCF carries no explicit closure charge, so we disclose the omitted liability rather than model it. The group carries a reclamation and mine-closure provision of US$6.9m at the last year-end (F22) with annual additions that are accretion, not the terminal closure cost, and the reserve statement depletes the disclosed base inside the horizon — so the DCF understates the tail by that closure cost [S3]. This is a known understatement rather than an unbudgeted one; it is stated here rather than shocked in the scenario, which keeps the two tails mirrored [S3].

Cash flow and the balance sheet. FY2025 capex was US$19.2m (F11), funded several times over by operating cash flow [S0]. The balance sheet is conservative: at the last year-end cash of US$112.1m against debt of US$134.4m left net debt / EBITDA of 0.1x, and by the 30 June 2026 balance sheet the group held more cash than debt [S0, S5]. The asset-light contractor model means working capital, not equipment, is the main use of cash [S0].

Capital allocation and dividend capacity. GEMS returns most of what it earns: FY2025 dividends paid were US$210.0m against parent net profit of US$258.2m, and FY2026 has already seen the US$200.0m interim declared and paid (F13) [S7]. From FY2027E we hold the payout at 0.8 of parent profit, the demonstrated record; for FY2026E the model's d.p.s. line is the remaining final tranche only, because the interim is already paid and bridged in the valuation section. The final tranche and the forward dividend are comfortably covered by forecast free cash flow, so the yield cross-check's much higher figure is a timing-and-rate artefact rather than a signal we can bank [S0, S7].

Earnings-quality flags. The accrual gap is measured, not asserted: operating cash flow was US$390.7m in FY2023 against net profit of US$528.7m, US$571.8m in FY2024 against US$483.1m, and US$246.9m in FY2025 against US$259.8m (F53, F54, F57) [S3, S8]. Set against total assets of US$1,196.6m at the last year-end and US$1,312.0m a year earlier (F55, F58), the FY2025 accrual gap is a very small fraction of the balance sheet and far narrower than in FY2023, when cash conversion was at its weakest; the trend is toward cash, so we classify the FY2025 gap as **explained** — a timing and depreciation-geography effect, not a revenue-recognition problem — and not manipulation-class [S3, S8]. Related-party flows moved sharply year on year and the LK does not explain the move: cost of revenue booked with related parties fell to 6.94% of the total in FY2025 (F15) from roughly a fifth the year before, and related-party revenue fell to US$33.9m (F23), down more than six-fold from the prior year, as the group's mining-services, hauling and management buying shifted toward the two third-party contractors above a tenth of revenue (F30). Because the flows are disclosed and the direction is toward third parties, we flag the channel optics-class rather than manipulation-class; but the swing in intra-group purchasing is a governance watch item, not a background constant [S3, S8]. The whole cash-cost calibration rides on the post-shift year, so we test a reversion rather than assume it away: the LK states that related-party terms may differ from third-party terms but discloses no price differential either way, and the FY2024 unit cash cost on the same identity (US$1,600.9m of cost of revenue less US$339.8m of royalty less US$12.7m of depreciation over 50.7 Mt) differs from the FY2025 level by only a small fraction, which bounds the mix effect; the bear case carries that bound as a cost shock so the reversion is priced, not argued [S3, S4]. Input-side concentration is the sharper flag: the group's own threshold disclosure names two mining contractors above a tenth of revenue in FY2025 — the largest at 22.0% of revenue — so contractor concentration is rising even though management states there is no concentration of sales to related parties, and the domestic book remains the majority of revenue (F10) [S3, S8]. No special-board status or going-concern notation is present [S0].

A cyclical producer is valued on the worth of its reserves at a through-cycle price — never on the current year's multiple — so the life-of-reserve DCF is our primary method and the multiples are cross-checks only. The DCF is a finite-life value cut at the licensed terms, not at the last tonne in the statement: the model runs the production years inside BORNEO's and BSL's CCoW terms and stops at FY2037E, so there is no terminal crutch and no tonne beyond a sourced licence is banked. The "dcf_life" line is the best-cumulative present value of that licensed stream — an honest peak, not an arbitrary truncation. It values the equity at Rp6,879. The WACC is 10.2%, from a risk-free rate of 4.9%, a mature-market equity premium of 4.2% and a country risk premium of 2.5%; the cost of equity is 10.5% and the pre-tax cost of debt is 6.9% [S0].

**Licence coverage and the reserve schedule.** We state the terms and value only inside them. The reserve statement splits the 844.4 Mt base by block (F3): BORNEO's 527.0 Mt (F48) and BSL's 183.8 Mt (F49) are the two coal-contract-of-work blocks, with the balance in the IUP holders, whose licences are short-dated — WRL's IUP Operasi Produksi was last extended only to 19 November 2027 (F50) [S3]. BORNEO's production stage began 17 February 2006 for a thirty-year term (to about February 2036, F38) and BSL's began 31 March 2011 for a thirty-year term (to about March 2041, F46). At the modelled sales rate the two CCoW reserves cover the twelve-year horizon, so the DCF stops at FY2037E: BORNEO's reserve is worked out inside its 2036 term and the FY2037E year is carried by BSL inside its 2041 term. The IUP tonnes would need extensions we have not sourced, so they are not valued; the unvalued IUP blocks and the residual BSL tonnes beyond FY2037E are disclosed upside, not a hidden base case. This is a deliberate, sourced truncation rather than a cautious haircut: nothing in the base depends on a renewal, and a failure to renew BORNEO past 2036 changes no modelled year [S3].

The cross-check agrees with the primary. On EV/EBITDA the name screens at Rp6,427, -6.6% versus the primary — close to the DCF, because the multiple is applied to the FY2025A EBITDA, a normal-year figure struck on the reported definition the peer multiples share, while the DCF prices the same resource through the cycle at the rebuilt, full-D&A EBITDA. The **dividend-yield cross-check stays excluded**: it capitalises the forward twelve-month DPS out of peak FY2026E earnings and therefore prices a figure the report itself calls a timing-and-rate artefact. Excluding it leaves the two through-cycle methods, renormalised to 71% DCF and 29% EV/EBITDA, so the target no longer depends on the payout persisting.

**The dividend anchor, stated against NAV, as the coal method requires.** IDX coal names trade on dividend capacity, so we say which anchor the market is using and which we use. The market's anchor is the dividend: at the last price the trailing twelve-month dividend yield is 11.9% [S0], and the group's demonstrated payout policy is 0.8 of parent profit — the market is capitalising a normal-year distribution, not our reserve NAV of Rp6,879. Our anchor is NAV at the through-cycle marker, which is why the share price sits above our fundamental value rather than below it. The two are not contradictory: a high normal-year payout on a finite reserve base can be capitalised at a high yield for as long as the reserve lasts, and the market is paying for the distribution stream while we value the reserve that funds it. If the dividend method were given a weight in the blend it would pull the target toward the price, not away from it — which is exactly why we leave it out when its forward dividend is a peak-year figure, and state the anchor here instead of letting an excluded method silently set the tone [S0, S3].

Under the blend, the fundamental twelve-month value is **Rp6,215** — the probability-weighted business scenarios, rolled forward at the cost of equity and net of the next twelve months' dividend, after the liquidity discount of 10.0% [S0]. The EV-to-equity bridge carries the balance-sheet items the operating DCF omits: we subtract the reclamation and mine-closure provision, add back the US$56.0m of long-term debt securities the group holds outside cash (F47), a non-operating asset in neither the reserve DCF nor the cash-less-debt net-debt leg [S5], and deduct the US$200.0m FY2026 interim paid on 22 October 2026 (F13), which left the company after the 30 June 2026 balance sheet so the net-cash leg does not reflect it — the same payment the forward dividend excludes, so it is counted once [S7]. Three further bridge items answer the review's valuation gaps. The blocks outside the two CCoW terms are carried at their sourced sunk book value rather than at zero — WRL at US$0.4m and the TBBU/KIM development block at US$1.6m (F51, F52) — because the house rule values a development project at least at what has been sunk into it; no DCF is applied because neither block produces and neither has a sourced development plan or licence term beyond WRL's 2,027 expiry. And the free-float remedy is priced as a bound, not left as an unquantified overhang: if the group lifts the public shareholding with new shares rather than a controller block sell-down, the new shares must equal the 2.4% gap divided by the retained stake of the enlarged count — a dilution a little larger than the raw gap, which we carry at half weight because the non-dilutive block-sale route is also open [S10, F45]. The reverse check is explicit and unit-bearing: holding our method fixed and solving for the Newcastle benchmark, the market price is consistent with a benchmark of US$123/t — obtained by scaling the deck's 118.0 USD/t marker by 1.04 until the DCF equals the market price. That is only a few percent above the deck's own FY2027E marker, so the market is pricing close to the deck's near-term path and far below spot: the war premium sits in the spot marker and in today's earnings, not in the share price. **Method note, disclosed rather than smoothed:** the reverse check and the two scenario tails are priced on the engine's repricing path, which scales the deck series without the deck's own long-run USD escalation; the base case carries that escalation, so the base is the firmer of the three and is the one we weight.

The sensitivity table shows the ranking the assumptions impose: the benchmark price underpinning the realised price moves value far more than volume or cost intensity, which is why we calibrate realisation on the FY2025A actual and never fit a ratio to a forecast-year spike. Two limits are carried honestly: the base DCF has no terminal value and no explicit mine-closure charge, so it may overstate value at the very end of the reserve life while understating it if the group proves up additional reserves or extends licence terms.

**The konglo lens — the regime step from fundamental value to target.** GEMS is a listed member of the Widjaja family's Sinar Mas group and sits on the exchange's HSC list [S9, S12], so the engine adds a lens that turns our fundamental value into the most likely twelve-month price. The lens measures the price against fundamental value today — 1.13×, i.e. a premium — and then keeps only part of that gap for twelve months, with the closing share rising with the name's regime flags. Two flags apply here: the HSC status, now formally operative from 2 November 2026 — the name is out of the IHSG, LQ45, IDX30 and IDX80 calculations (while still trading normally), so the domestic passive index demand is removed [S15, S16, S18]; the konglo registry records no GEMS deletion from the MSCI indexes, and we therefore make no MSCI claim — and a free-float step due inside the window — the float is 10.1% against a rule that requires 12.5% by 31 March 2027, a gap of 2.4% points about 4.9 months out [S10]. Because the price sits above value, the lens does not add value the way it would for a name trading below fundamental value: it keeps only part of the premium, so the target of Rp6,721 sits above the fundamental value of Rp6,215 but below the price. The base regime case closes 40.0% of the log gap and lands at Rp6,705. This is a target adjustment, not a valuation input: the fundamental work above is unchanged by it, and we do not bend either the price or the reserve DCF to pre-empt the regime [S0, S9, S10]. The 2 November implementation changes none of that arithmetic: the lens already carried the HSC exclusion as a flag, and the effective date confirms the flag rather than adding a new one, so the target is unchanged by the news even though the flow backdrop around it is now a fact rather than a prospect [S15, S16].

**Group context / SOTP.** GEMS is an operating miner, not a holdco: it holds no listed equity stakes, so there is no sibling SOTP to build inside this report — the direction of consolidation runs the other way. Its coal business is majority-owned and consolidated by PT Dian Swastatika Sentosa (DSSA), the Sinar Mas coal-and-infrastructure holdco covered by the house in its own note (`coverage/companies/DSSA.JK/report.md`); **no DSSA rating or target number enters this report's valuation** — GEMS is the operating subsidiary, valued on its own reserve DCF, not a stake marked inside a SOTP [S3]. The group-level SOTP runs at DSSA, whose model marks GEMS as a `method: house` holding at GEMS's own house value rather than at market (`coverage/companies/DSSA.JK/assumptions.yaml`, holdings block), so the parent and the covered subsidiary read the same number from the same direction.

Regulatory risk is high-likelihood, medium-impact: the royalty regime is set administratively and the dominant lever is the licence class — GEMS's contract-of-work terms fix its royalty today, and any change to the contract-to-IUPK transition would move the state's take; RKAB production quotas are the sector's supply lever and can cap or redirect volume [S3]. Macro and commodity risk is high-likelihood, high-impact: the realised price is the single largest driver, and a normalisation of the premium lifting the Newcastle marker would cut revenue straight through to the dividend [S-deck]. Operational risk — contractor cost inflation and performance on weaker units — is medium-likelihood, medium-impact, and the group has taken impairment charges on weaker cash-generating units [S3]. FX risk is medium-likelihood, low-to-medium impact: revenues are largely USD while part of the cost base is rupiah [S3]. Governance and liquidity risk is elevated: the free float is a small fraction of the capital and the controlling group sets strategy, so exits are thin; we capture this with the liquidity discount of 10.0% in the target [S0, S3].

**Licence-term risk is handled by exclusion, not by a haircut.** The base values only the two sourced CCoW blocks — BORNEO 527.0 Mt (F48), term to about Feb 2036 (F38); BSL 183.8 Mt (F49), term to about Mar 2041 (F46) — and stops at FY2037E. The IUP blocks are outside it, because WRL's licence was last extended only to 19 November 2027 (F50) and the group has disclosed no further extension, and the residual BSL tonnes beyond the cut are also unvalued. So a renewal failure costs no modelled year; the live exposure is the other way — the excluded tonnes and any CCoW extension are upside we have not paid for — and the post-2036 tail we do value needs BSL to carry it inside its 2041 term. That is the explicit bear-side reading of the licence: no extension value is banked, and none is double-counted in the bear [S3].
**Business scenarios** (

). Bear (probability 25.0%): the benchmark settles well below the deck's path, a DMO-plus-RKAB clamp trims FY2026 volume a few percent below the company's 58.0 Mt target, the realised-to-benchmark ratio slips a further two points as the mix shifts to lower-value domestic tonnes, and the unit cash cost reverts to the FY2024 level as intra-group purchasing returns to its earlier share (the bounded cost-mix reversion set out in the financial section) — value Rp2,092. Base (50.0%): the modelled through-cycle price path holds and the royalty is charged at the contract rate — value Rp6,652. Bull (25.0%): the marker's premium proves structural and the deck's long-run path is too low, the 58.0 Mt target is delivered and modestly exceeded, the realised-to-benchmark ratio gains a couple of points as higher-value offtake improves the mix, and contractor competition holds the unit cost at the FY2025 level with the mix not reverting — value Rp12,228. The two tails shock the same four drivers by mirrored amounts, so what separates them is the state of the coal complex and its cost base, not a stack of cautious assumptions.

**Why these probabilities, and what a heavier bear does.** The weighting is not symmetry by default. The base case is modal because the deck's through-cycle marker sits at its own long-run level, the FY2025A realised ratio is a normal-year ratio rather than a trough fit, and the LK's own cost base supports the margin — but the price sits above our fundamental value, the HSC exclusion is effective the day after our valuation date, the free-float step is due inside the horizon and the parent faces a criminal-path consideration, which is why the bear is not shaded below the bull. We keep the base at the modal weight and the two tails equal because the shocks are mirrored and the evidence does not support tilting one tail more than the other. The cushion is thin: our own run with the bear weighted materially higher than the base case's quarter — the direction the market's premium would justify — takes the total return below zero and the rating to REDUCE, so the HOLD survives only on the central weighting and on the undeclared final dividend. That is stated rather than hidden: this is a dividend bet with a thin cushion, not a re-rating call [S0, S9, S10, S17].

**The reserve base is modelled as closed and licence-bounded.** Both tails move the same four drivers and neither adds reserves or extends a licence. That is the most-likely read, not a missing lever: the LK's own reserve roll-forward shows the base drawn down by production with no net additions over FY2024 and FY2025 (949.9 → 899.2 → 844.4 Mt, F24/F4/F3), the desk method excludes exploration value from the base NAV, and the DCF stops at the sourced CCoW terms (F38, F46, F48, F49). A coal name's reserve-addition and licence-extension options are real, but they are unsourced here, so the bull expresses demand-side strength — price, mix, volume and payout — rather than reserve growth, and we disclose the omission instead of capitalising it [S3].

**The konglo-regime scenarios are separate from the business scenarios** and are what turn fundamental value into the target. The engine's regime deck runs three cases over the same twelve months: bear (80.0% of the gap closes — the deck's own stress, e.g. a Standalone reclassification or forced placements at deep discounts), base (40.0%) and bull (-5.0%, a negative number meaning the gap re-expands in a relief rally). Weighting those cases gives the target Rp6,721, above the fundamental Rp6,215 and below the price. The regime catalysts are dated: HSC names, GEMS included, formally leave the IHSG, LQ45, IDX30 and IDX80 on 2 November 2026 — the removal is effective and the shares keep trading normally [S15, S16, S18] — with a quarterly HSC review, the free float must reach the first step of the rule by 31 March 2027, and MSCI takes feedback on its Indonesia Standalone proposal until 30 April 2027 with a decision by 30 June 2027 [S10, S11, S13]. The reading we hold is that the most likely path keeps only part of the premium: the HSC exclusion becomes effective on 2 November 2026 — the session after our valuation date — so the passive outflow is **ahead**, not behind, and we do not claim it is complete; no sourced index weight or tracker-flow estimate exists to size it, so we treat it as a live regime headwind rather than a spent event, and the free-float deadline is a second structural overhang inside the horizon, so we do not assume the full premium persists [S9, S10, S11, S15, S16]. The parent-level OJK criminal-path consideration is a separate governance event, not a change to this subsidiary's cash flows [S17].

Signposts that would change our view: a sustained marker above the deck's long-run level; a material shift in the sales mix toward higher-value offtake; a royalty-regime change that moves GEMS's licences onto a different schedule; a BORNEO CCoW extension past its 2036 production term, or a further IUP renewal such as WRL's November 2027 term (F50) — both would add tonnes we have deliberately left outside the base rather than value we have already banked; a step-up in free float ahead of the March 2027 deadline (a controller sell-down or new shares, which would cut the konglo overhang); or a change of control at the DSSA level [S3, S10].

Risk ranked by likelihood times impact. The dominant risk is the realised price — the largest driver, and the one the market is least worried about because the share price sits near the deck's own path while the war premium still sits in spot. The royalty is a quieter second now priced off the contract, and balance-sheet risk is low given the group's cash [S0]. The honest bear case is not a solvency story but a dividend-capacity one: if the through-cycle price is where our DCF says it is, the generous payout is funded by a price that will not persist. The honest bull case is that the war premium is structural — Chinese import discipline and Indonesian supply restraint — in which case the deck's long-run marker is too low and both the DCF and the dividend prove conservative. Two sensitivities sit alongside: the realised-to-benchmark ratio is held flat at its FY2025A level against a Newcastle marker of 108.4 USD/t, so a shift in the sales mix (which moves the ratio) swings value more than volume does; and the payout is modelled at the group's demonstrated record rather than below it, so a cut — not the standing four-fifths rate — is what would change the dividend stream. We weight the bear and bull at the probabilities shown and take the base case as the modal outcome.

**The konglo profile.** GEMS is controlled by the Widjaja family through the Sinar Mas group: the LK states the company operates under the Sinarmas group of businesses, that its direct parent is PT Dian Swastatika Sentosa Tbk (DSSA) and that its ultimate controlling shareholders are Franky Oesman Widjaja and Indra Widjaja [S3]. Its role in the group is the listed coal operating vehicle. The share register shows how concentrated the capital is: DSSA holds 51.0% and PT Radhika Jananta Raya 30.0%, with Golden Energy and Resources Pte. Ltd. of Singapore at 7.0% and the public at 10.4% (F40-F43) [S3]. There is no disclosed share pledge in the LK we searched, and no related-party sales concentration is flagged as a red line; the related-party channel is on the cost side — mining services, hauling and management from affiliates, 6.94% of cost of revenue in FY2025 (F15), down sharply from about a fifth the year before, with related-party revenue also down more than six-fold to US$33.9m (F23) — an optics-class flag we monitor, and a swing in intra-group purchasing that the LK does not explain [S3].

Free float and the konglo regime. The free float the lens measures on is the current figure of 10.1% (F45) [S14], as of 26 October 2026, taken from a market-data vendor that mirrors the exchange's registry rather than from the exchange itself, a little below the LK's 31 December 2025 register figure of 10.4% (F42) — the float drifted down over 2026 — and both sit below the exchange's minimum. Under the tiered rule a large-cap below the first threshold must reach the first step by 31 March 2027 and the second by 31 March 2028 [S10]. The gap to the first step is 2.4% of the capital and 4.9 months out; the group can close it either by a controller sell-down of roughly that share of the capital or by a marginally larger new-share issue (issuing shares also lifts the denominator, so slightly more must come to market than the raw gap implies), and the lens prices that overhang as a regime factor — its free-float adjustment — not as a fundamental input [S10, S14]. The two routes are not equivalent for the shareholder. A market sell-down of the gap would take years at the stock's average daily turnover, so the practical routes are a controller block sale to institutions or a new-share issue; the block sale moves no per-share value, while the new-share route dilutes by the gap measured against the retained stake and is carried in the valuation bridge at half weight. We assume no route in the base case because none is announced — the post-balance-sheet search found no issue, placement or rights issue — and the per-share dilution is therefore priced as a bound, not as a base-case haircut [S5, S7, S10]. GEMS is on the exchange's HSC list [S9], and Sinar Mas is the group with the most names on that list — five, including DSSA and GEMS [S12, F44] — so from 2 November 2026 the HSC names, GEMS included, are out of the IHSG, LQ45, IDX30 and IDX80 while still trading normally and without delisting [S15, S16, S18, F44]. MSCI opened a consultation on reclassifying Indonesia to Standalone Market status on 15 October 2026, with its freeze on Indonesian index increases in place until further notice and a decision due by 30 June 2027 [S11]. No enforcement action against GEMS itself is recorded: the konglo registry's ticker table carries the 2026 OJK manipulation case against the parent DSSA but has no GEMS entry, so the penalties in the wider Sinar Mas complex fell on other parties, not on GEMS (`coverage/universe/konglo.yaml`, tickers block). On 1 November 2026 OJK said it is weighing a criminal path, under the single-track (*una via*) regime, in the same DSSA/BREN/CUAN case, after the administrative fines already imposed [S17]; GEMS is not among the named issuers and the proceeding sits at the parent level, so we treat it as a governance watch item and do not import the parent's own share-price view into this report — the subsidiary is valued on its own reserve DCF [S17]. That independence is argued, not asserted: a DSSA-level sanction could reach GEMS through four channels. First, a forced or voluntary sale of the parent's 51.0% stake (F40) would be a free-float event and a possible change of control, which under the tender-offer regime would set a price floor and a dated catalyst. Second, the group could raise cash at GEMS to fund parent-level liabilities — a higher dividend call or an intercompany loan — which would not change our fundamental value but would change the distribution timing. Third, enforcement contagion could freeze the group's capital-markets agenda inside the free-float window, making the new-share route harder rather than easier. Fourth, the same HSC and index treatment that already applies to the parent applies to GEMS, so a further MSCI or exchange action at the group level would hit both. None of these changes a modelled cash flow today, and none has a sourced probability, so we assign them zero modelled value and watch three triggers: any change in DSSA's disclosed stake, any GEMS dividend or loan that exceeds the demonstrated payout policy, and any OJK step naming a GEMS entity or a GEMS director [S3, S17, S10]. There are no index deletions of GEMS recorded in the regime registry we read.

Auditor and opinion. The FY2025 statements are audited by Mirawati Sensi Idris with an unqualified opinion; key audit matters centre on asset impairment and goodwill testing [S3]. No special-notation letter or special-monitoring-board status is present [S0].

Dividend record. The company has a long and consistent dividend record and pays out most of its parent profit; the FY2026 interim (F13) was declared and paid on 22 October 2026 and continues that policy [S7]. On group cash needs, the parent DSSA is the group's coal-and-infrastructure holdco and is itself covered by the house, so the coal leg's dividend is best read as the group's call on GEMS's cash rather than a fixed policy [S3].

ESG. The material exposures are mine rehabilitation and closure obligations — a provision is carried on the balance sheet [S3] — dust and water management at mine sites, and the sector-level carbon-transition risk that pressures the long-run thermal price [S3]. Governance is the binding ESG factor here, given concentrated control and intra-group cost flows (F15) [S0].

Dated catalysts are in the frontmatter: the HSC removal from the IHSG, LQ45, IDX30 and IDX80, operative from 2 November 2026 with the quarterly HSC review [S15, S16, S18, F44]; the FY2026 volume outcome against the company target (F14) [S6]; the free-float step to 12.5% by 31 March 2027 [S10]; MSCI's feedback close on 30 April 2027 and the Standalone decision by 30 June 2027 [S11]; the FY2026 audited statements and the final dividend (the only FY2026 dividend in our forward return, since the October interim is already paid); and the licence calendar — WRL's IUP term ends 19 November 2027 (F50) and BORNEO's CCoW production stage in February 2036 (F38), both of which sit outside the base and would add tonnes only if renewed. Between updates we monitor the government reference prices and the Newcastle marker against our long-run assumption; the quarterly production and sales disclosures; the royalty line in the LK as a check on our modelled contract rate — the expense line (F59), not the cash paid, which includes advance-royalty timing (F7); the dividend declarations and payout, with the FY2026 final declaration the single most important event for the call; the free float and any placement or block sale; the annual reserve statement; and any change in DSSA-level ownership, free float or the group's coal consolidation, including any spill of the parent-level OJK criminal-path consideration into GEMS's ownership or float [S17].

The KPIs we watch, and why. First, the realised-to-benchmark ratio: it is our largest value driver and the easiest to falsify, so we track the reported realised price each quarter against the ratio we hold flat. Second, the royalty line: it is the cleanest early read on whether the contract rate we charge is the rate being paid, and a persistent gap — or a move to a different licence schedule — would force us to revisit the reconciliation. Third, volume against the company target: the reserve base is finite, so the sales pace sets the length of the cash-flow stream the DCF discounts. Fourth, cash cost per tonne: strip ratio and contractor pricing are undisclosed, so cost of revenue is the only check on our intensity and haulage assumptions. Fifth, the dividend: the payout is the market's anchor, so any cut or step-up is a signal about management's own price view. And now, with the konglo lens, the free float itself: a step toward the first free-float floor — a controller sell-down or a placement — is the dated event that moves the regime reading most, so we watch the monthly share register alongside it [S3, S10].

assumptions.label: Sales volume plan
assumptions.basis: FY2026E is the company's own production-and-sales target of up to 58 Mt (F14), +5.6% on the 54.9 Mt FY2025A actual (F1); we hold FY2027E-30E flat at 58 Mt — the company's own disclosed pace, corroborated by H1 FY2026 production of 28.7 Mt (F34, the LK's July-2026 reserve roll-forward, an annual rate of about 57 Mt), then flat into lt. No capacity, RKAB or reserve-addition source supports a step above the company plan, so none is taken (round-2 C5). The reserve base of 844.4 Mt (F3) leaves roughly fourteen years of life at this rate, so the engine's reserves line caps the tail well inside the horizon. Deviation from the starter belief: the starter carried the last actual (54.9) forward; we adopt the disclosed target because it is the company's own plan and the LK's reserve reconciliation already assumes production of that order.

assumptions.label: Realised price / benchmark
assumptions.basis: Calibrated on the FY2025A actual, exactly as the desk rule requires: realised price US$43.94/t (revenue US$2,414.1m (F10) / 54.9 Mt (F1)) over the FY2025A Newcastle 6,000 NAR average of 108.4 US$/t = 0.405. FY2025A is a NORMAL price year, NOT a trough: the deck's FY2025A marker of 108.4 sits marginally ABOVE the deck's own long-run level (FY2029E 105.0 and lt 105.0), so 0.405 is a normal-year realised-to-benchmark ratio held flat — a plain most-likely input, not a conservative haircut, and the bull therefore does not rest on a mean-reversion of a depressed ratio (round-3 C5). We hold it flat across FY2026E-30E and lt and do NOT fit it to the FY2026E benchmark spike (137.0). Benchmark basis (why NOT the deck's HBA series, round-3 C1): the pinned COAL params set price_driver d.coal.newc (operating configuration SECTOR_LEAD_ENERGY) and the engine's calibration gate prices FY+1 off that driver's FY2025A value (108.4), which only newc carries; the deck's reviewed `hba` series is the high-GAR 6,322 kcal reference — the wrong grade for GEMS's low-CV product — and the correctly-graded HBA I (5,300) / II (4,100) / III (3,400) are spot-only with no forecast path, while the ICI indices are needs_source. So newc is the only reviewed coal series with both an FY actual (for the calibration) and a through-cycle path, the whole product discount stays in this realisation input, and the name stays consistent with the COAL batch. The discount reflects GEMS's low-CV product and its large domestic offtake (US$1,558.9m of US$2,414.1m revenue in FY2025 was domestic, F10).

assumptions.label: Share of volume under a price cap (e.g. DMO)
assumptions.basis: ENGINE-DEFAULT PROXY, not a sourced fact: domestic sales were 64.6% of FY2025 revenue by sales area (F10) but the LK does not disclose the power-station versus industrial split of the domestic book, so there is no fact, quote or locator for a 30% power-tonnage share. Marked default:true accordingly and INERT: the US$70/t dmo_cap sits above the modelled realised price (F10/F1 imply the FY2025A ASP), so min(cap, asp) binds nothing and the input does not move value at the modelled prices. The downside it would capture at higher prices is tested instead through the bear volume shock (DMO-plus-RKAB quota cap, C9). Kept as an insurance input only.

assumptions.label: Strip ratio (bcm per tonne) or cost-intensity factor
assumptions.basis: Not disclosed by GEMS; set at 4.0 bcm/t, in line with the group's own coal book (parent DSSA runs 4.9 and the peer set 4.0-4.9), and used only as the intensity factor that multiplies cost_per_bcm to rebuild the calibrated cash cost. Held flat.

assumptions.label: Mining cost per bcm (or per unit when intensity is 1)
assumptions.basis: US$3.0/bcm, the group/sector norm for Indonesian open-pit contractor mining (parent DSSA US$3.2/bcm), chosen so that strip_ratio x cost_per_bcm = US$12.0/t and, with other_cost_unit, lands the FY2025A cash cost on the LK. Cost inflates with Brent (fuel_driver) via fuel_share.

assumptions.label: Other cash cost per unit (haul, barge, process)
assumptions.basis: US$11.6/t: the balancing item that brings total cash cost to the LK-calibrated US$23.5/t. Derivation: FY2025A COGS US$1,642.8m (S3) less royalty US$312.4m (F7) less the full D&A charge of US$37.1m (F16) = US$1,293.3m; divided by 54.9 Mt (F1) = US$23.55/t cash cost; less strip_ratio x cost_per_bcm (4.0 x 3.0 = 12.0) = 11.55. Held flat. The calibration inherits the same D&A residual as da_unit: subtracting the segment-total D&A (F16) rather than the notes-based component sum (about US$32.66m, F5+F20+F21+F28+F29+F33) puts the unit cash cost about US$0.08/t too low, so the base case's other_cost_unit is calibrated at the segment-total end and the BEAR case adds that residual per tonne back (+0.08) with da_unit lowered to its notes-based end (round-2 L1) — both ends of the unexplained tenth are run and shown.

assumptions.label: Fuel share of mining cost
assumptions.basis: engine default constant — GEMS does not break out fuel; sector norm retained

assumptions.label: Royalty rate — PKP2B contract share-of-production the LK discloses
assumptions.basis: The rate the LK shows being PAID, reconciled to the contract (licence: PKP2B routes the engine to a FLAT rate). Royalty charged inside cost of revenues was US$312.449m in FY2025 (F7) on revenue of US$2,414.054m (F10) — an effective 12.94% of revenue — US$339.787m in FY2024 (12.6%, F8) and US$452.211m in FY2023 (15.6%, F31). BORNEO's CCoW states a 13.5% share of coal produced (F9, Note 37, S3), bracketed by that three-year effective history; we charge the FY2025A effective rate flat because a production share valued at the government reference is not the same thing as a share of realised revenue, and the LK's own cost-of-revenues line is where that conversion is actually booked (round-2 C3). This is the most-likely read, not the cautious one: the earlier build never stated a licence and charged the top IUPK band (18%) on the ex-PKP2B schedule by assertion, which overstated cost and understated value. GEMS is not an IUPK holder, so that schedule does not apply (the deck's IUPK note names its own holders, S3); royalty sensitivities at the 12.6% FY2024 low and the 15.6% FY2023 high bound the rate.

assumptions.label: Other revenue
assumptions.basis: engine default constant — no separately disclosed other-revenue stream

assumptions.label: Gross margin on other revenue
assumptions.basis: engine default constant

assumptions.label: D&A per unit (reporting currency)
assumptions.basis: Set on the FULL charge, US$0.676/t = the LK's own consolidated D&A of US$37.1m FY2025 (F16, Note 34) divided by 54.9 Mt (F1). We do NOT use the income-statement depreciation line alone (US$16.5m, F5): F5 is CONTAINED IN F16, so a reader must not add them — F16 is the segment total, F5 its income-statement property-and-equipment depreciation component. The notes-based bridge of that total is now: F5 (income-statement depreciation) + F20 (mine-property amortisation, producing mines) + F21 (stripping-activity amortisation) + F28 (business-combination mine-property amortisation in "Others - net") + F29 (the FULL intangible amortisation, US$27,864 cost of revenues PLUS US$1,209 G&A, a slice the earlier cost-of-revenues-only reading of the bridge missed) + F33 (right-of-use depreciation US$213,976, which the income-statement property-and-equipment allocation F5 does not contain). That component sum is US$32.66m against F16's US$37.12m — a residual of about a tenth of the segment total which the LK does not itemise (round-2 L1). ROUND-2 HEDGE: rather than carry that residual unhedged, da_unit is BOUNDED at both ends of it and the reader sees both values. The BASE uses the segment-total end (US$0.676/t, the fuller charge, which with the cash-cost identity also sets the lower calibrated other_cost_unit — see that input). The BEAR case runs the notes-based end (segment total less the residual, da_unit x0.875) TOGETHER with the matching cash-cost re-calibration (other_cost_unit + the residual per tonne), so the bear carries the whole unexplained tenth through BOTH channels — the D&A tax shield and the cash-cost calibration — and the value impact is visible in the scenario table. The four-year segment-note path is 19.17m / 60.53m / 0.57m / 37.12m (F27/F19/F18/F16) on production of 46.1 / 50.7 / 54.9 Mt (F25/F26/F1): FY2023's charge was inflated by a mine-property amortisation of US$24.8m (F20 FY2024 comparative) plus a US$24.1m mine-property impairment booked the prior year, while FY2024's 0.57m is anomalous against even that year's own Note 9 depreciation (F6), so no single year is a safe anchor. We therefore take the FY2025 full charge (F16) as the least-distorted full year, rebuild FY2024 from the notes (F6) and hold 0.676/t flat in real terms — a stated choice, not a spike fit.

assumptions.label: Sustaining capex per unit (reporting currency)
assumptions.basis: FY2025A capital expenditure of US$19.2m (F11) / 54.9 Mt (F1) = US$0.35/t. GEMS runs an asset-light contractor model, so capex is a small fraction of revenue; held flat.

assumptions.basis: engine default: average of FY2023A, FY2024A, FY2025A (div(interest_income, cash[-1]))

assumptions.basis: engine default constant — FX and other below-the-line items left at zero

assumptions.basis: engine default: average of FY2023A, FY2024A, FY2025A (div(minority, np)); FY2025 was 0.6% (F17)

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: The 0.80 policy is the demonstrated record: GEMS averaged ~0.81 of parent net profit over FY2023-25 (range 0.45-1.08), so 0.80 is the record, not a haircut below it (QC round-3 Q7). FY2026E is set to 0.453 as a TIMING input, not a policy change (QC round-3 Q6): the US$200m interim (Rp611.93/share, F13) was declared and paid on 22 October 2026, before this valuation date, so the cash a buyer at today's price still receives inside twelve months is the FY2026 final tranche only — the engine's dps line (and therefore val.dps12) is set to that residual, while the interim is deducted from equity in the bridge. FY2027E onwards returns to the 0.80 policy. The bull carries 0.95 to test the demonstrated ~1.0 payout ceiling; the bear 0.65.

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: Held at zero on the last actual, which is the base-case rule: no new-share issue, rights issue or placement is announced, and the post-balance-sheet search found none [S5, S7]. The free-float rule that has to be met by 31 March 2027 allows either a controller sell-down or a new-share issue, and the share register shows the controller group still above four-fifths of the capital, so a block sell-down is the non-dilutive route available [S10, F40-F43]. The dilution route is bounded rather than assumed: its value is carried in the valuation bridge at a probability, not in this per-share input, so the base case does not haircut the share count for a corporate action that has not been announced (review C3).

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: Zero: the DCF is a finite life-of-reserve value at the deck's long-run price and the engine's reserves line truncates production before the horizon end, so no perpetuity growth is added (consistent with the COAL peer convention).

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: Held at the historical average (0.166): FY2025 selling expenses of US$255.2m, G&A of US$147.6m and exploration of US$1.8m against US$2,414.1m revenue = 16.8%. Selling expenses include the barge/haulage and royalty-linked marketing costs, so they are broadly proportional to revenue.

challenges.challenge: 133.6 Mt of the 844.4 Mt reserve base (F3) - 15.8% - is valued at zero in both the base and the bull: WRL 87.2 Mt (F50), KIM 45.8 Mt and TKS 0.6 Mt sit outside BORNEO 527.0 Mt (F48) and BSL 183.8 Mt (F49), and the residual BSL tonnes beyond FY2037E are also unvalued. WRL is not a dormant exploration block but an IUP Operasi Produksi (F50). The method card says value everything the company owns and never carry an asset at zero; the report discloses the omission but neither the base nor the bull pays anything for it. The model also runs the group's 58 Mt production-and-sales target (F14) and depletes the full 844.4 Mt reserve line to 148.4 Mt at FY2037E, so the claim that only CCoW tonnes are mined is a narrative overlay, not a model switch - if WRL produces, the CCoW-only reserve life is shorter than 12 years.
challenges.answer: The IUP and development blocks are no longer carried at zero. The LK's own reserve table assigns carrying values: WRL's 87.2 Mt is an exploration-and-evaluation asset with US$0.43m booked and no FY2025 production, and the TBBU/KIM 45.8 Mt is a mine under construction with US$1.61m booked. Both enter the valuation bridge at those sourced sunk-cost floors (new F51/F52), per the house rule that a development project is worth at least its sunk capex; neither gets a DCF because neither produces and neither has a sourced development plan. The bull keeps mirrored demand-side shocks and does not bank an extension we cannot source; the licence lever is disclosed as upside above the floor. The reserve-line point is answered in the financial section: the DCF stops at 12 years and 696 Mt, inside the 710.8 Mt of CCoW tonnes, and the reserve counter is accounting depletion, not a claim that WRL or TBBU produce.

challenges.challenge: The COAL card's output contract requires a dividend-capacity-yield-versus-NAV anchor statement - which anchor the market is using and which the report is using - because IDX coal names trade on dividend capacity. The report zero-weights the dividend method (justified as an FY2026E peak-payout artefact) but never states the normal-year anchor: FY2025A dividends paid were US$210.0m, an 8.8% yield on the US$2,394m market cap, and the report itself says the whole 2.4% total return is dividend-carried. Excluding the method without showing the through-cycle yield leaves the reader unable to see whether the market is pricing a normal-year dividend yield well above the house's NAV.
challenges.answer: Added the dividend-capacity-yield-versus-NAV anchor statement to section 4: the market's anchor is the trailing dividend yield at the last price and the demonstrated payout policy; our anchor is the reserve NAV. The paragraph states that a normal-year dividend method would pull the target toward the price rather than away, which is why the peak-year forward-dividend method stays excluded, and why the two anchors can coexist on a finite reserve base.

challenges.challenge: The free-float non-compliance (10.08% versus 12.5% by 31 March 2027, a 2.42-point gap, registry S25/S10) is described as an overhang but never valued. 2.42% of 5,882.353m shares is ~142.4m shares; at the Rp1.75bn/day ADTV that is roughly 600 trading days to absorb through the market. If the group instead issues shares to lift the public to 12.5%, the new-share requirement is ~2.77% of the enlarged count (2.42/(100-12.5)), about Rp182/share or 2.7% of the Rp6,749 target. The model keeps share_change at the engine default 0.0 with no source, and the report never says which route it assumes or what it costs.
challenges.answer: The free-float remedy is now valued and the route stated. Base share_change stays at zero because no issue, rights issue or placement is announced and the post-balance-sheet search found none, with a full basis and sources added. The new-share route is bounded in the bridge: the gap is 2.77% of the enlarged count, about US$55m on a US$2.0bn fundamental equity value, carried at 0.5 probability because a non-dilutive controller block sale is the alternative. Section 6 states that a market sell-down would take years at ADTV, so the practical routes are a block sale or a new issue, and prices dilution as a bound, not a base haircut.

challenges.challenge: The report says "the forced index selling is at its effective date and largely done", but the HSC exclusion takes effect Monday 2 November 2026 - the day after the 1 November asof - and no source is given for "largely done". There is no estimate of GEMS's weight in the IHSG/LQ45/IDX30/IDX80 or of the passive assets that must sell on the rebalance, although the claim supports the base 40% closing share and the 25% bear probability. S15/S18 establish the effective date and the list, not that the flow is complete.
challenges.answer: Deleted the "largely done" claim. The report now states that the HSC exclusion takes effect on 2 November 2026, the session after the valuation date, so the passive outflow is ahead, not behind; no sourced index weight or tracker-flow estimate exists, so the event is treated as a live regime headwind rather than a spent one. The konglo lens parameters are the deck's and were not changed.

challenges.challenge: The forward Rp804 dividend is a model residual - FY2026E payout 0.453 x parent profit (0.80 total payout less the US$200m interim) - not a declared or guided payment, yet the summary calls it "the FY2026 final dividend ... payable by the IDX norm on 30 June 2027". It is 96% of the 2.4% total return: a 10.9% yield offsetting an 8.5% fall to target. The FY2023-25 payout range in the model is 0.45-1.08 (FY2024 was 0.447); at the low end the final tranche would be near zero and the rating would be REDUCE on the same target.
challenges.answer: The summary and section 4 now state that the final tranche is undeclared and unguided: it is the model residual of the demonstrated payout over FY2026 parent profit after the interim, and it carries nearly the whole total return. The report states that at the low end of the group's own payout record the final tranche would shrink toward nothing and the call would move to REDUCE, and section 5 calls the HOLD a dividend bet with a thin cushion that survives only on the central weighting and the undeclared final.

challenges.challenge: The model charges royalty at 12.9% of revenue (the FY2025A effective rate), but the most recent LK shows H1 FY2026 royalty and deadrent paid of US$203.43m (F37) on revenue of US$1,495.28m (F35) - 13.60%, about 0.7pp higher. On FY2026E revenue of US$3,218m that is ~US$437.6m versus the model's ~US$415.1m, ~US$22.5m of extra cost (about 2.8% of FY2026E EBITDA), repeated across the DCF for roughly 2-3% of value (~Rp150-190/share). The report's §7 names the royalty line as the quarterly check but tests only F7, not F37.
challenges.answer: The 13.6% figure compares a cash-paid line with an accrual revenue base. F37 is royalty fees AND deadrent PAID; the S5 note shows the royalty EXPENSE inside cost of revenues for H1 FY2026 was US$192.134m (new F59) against H1 revenue of US$1,495.283m (F35) - 12.85%, in line with the modelled 12.9%. The US$11.3m difference is the advance-royalty step-up (US$0.29m to US$11.51m at the two balance-sheet dates) plus a small accrued-royalty movement; deadrent for the half was US$54,815, immaterial and booked in G&A, not cost of revenues. The rate is the expense rate the LK shows being charged, so no royalty change was made.

challenges.challenge: The HOLD has only a 2.4% expected-return cushion, and the 25/50/25 weighting is asserted without a probability rationale. Moving 10pp from base to bear (35/45/20) cuts the probability-weighted business value from US$6,800m to about US$6,122m and the target to roughly Rp6,080, taking total return to about -7% (REDUCE). challenges.answer: Added a probability-rationale paragraph: the base is modal because the through-cycle marker is at its long-run level, the FY2025A realisation is a normal-year ratio and the LK cost base supports the margin, while the premium to fundamental value, the operative HSC exclusion, the looming free-float step and the parent's criminal-path consideration keep the bear at the bull's weight. The report states that a materially heavier bear weight takes total return below zero and the rating to REDUCE, and that the HOLD is a dividend bet with a thin cushion. Shocks remain mirrored; probabilities unchanged at 25/50/25.

challenges.challenge: Related-party COGS fell from 19.13% to 6.94% of total cost of revenue in one year (F15) and related-party revenue fell 6.9x to US$33.9m (F23), and the LK does not explain the move - the report calls it optics-class. challenges.answer: The cost-mix reversion is now priced, not argued. Section 3 shows the LK states related-party terms may differ from third-party terms with no price differential disclosed, and bounds the effect with the FY2024 unit cash cost on the same identity (FY2024 COGS less royalty less D&A over volume), which differs from FY2025 by only a small fraction. The bear's fourth shock is now a unit-cost reversion of +US$0.55/t, mirrored by -US$0.55/t in the bull; the payout shocks were removed because payout does not drive DCF value and was inverting the tails through retained cash.

Section 6 now describes S14 as a market-data vendor that mirrors the exchange registry, not the exchange registry itself.

Each has zero modelled value today because none changes a modelled cash flow and none has a sourced probability; three monitorable triggers are named.

The 6.5% FY2025A calibration gap (engine 403.56 vs pack 378.93) is a pack D&A-basis artefact: on the LK full D&A (F16 37.12m) the rebuild is US$403.8m versus the pack 378.93m, within 0.1%. §3 states both bases, so the gap is explained.

Bear value 2,092 is 32% of base and bull 12,226 is 184%: mirrored driver shocks still produce an asymmetric value outcome through operating leverage. Probabilities are 25/50/25 and the asymmetry is disclosed; no defect.

flags.message: a.payout moves +34.7pp from FY2026E to FY2037E: source the change or hold it
flags.justification: The FY2026E payout input is a dividend-timing adjustment, not a policy change (QC round-3 Q6): the US$200m interim (Rp611.93/share) was declared and paid on 22 Oct 2026 (S7, F13), before the 27 Oct valuation date, so the engine's FY2026E dps line is the remaining final tranche and the interim sits in the valuation bridge; FY2027E onward returns to the 0.80 record payout [S7, F13].

flags.message: PKP2B royalty is contract-specific: set a.royalty_rate to the rate the contract or LK shows and justify it with that source
flags.justification: a.royalty_rate is the PKP2B rate the LK shows being PAID: royalty inside cost of revenues was US$312.449m FY2025 (F7) on revenue of US$2,414.054m (F10) — an effective 12.94% of revenue — US$339.787m FY2024 (12.6%, F8) and US$452.211m FY2023 (15.6%, F31), bracketing BORNEO's stated 13.5% CCoW share of coal produced (F9, S3). PP 15/2022 Art. 14(2) keeps a PKP2B on its contract PNBP terms and the LK books the charge as a share of realised revenue, so the FY2025A effective rate is the most-likely input and no deck IUPK schedule applies to this licence class.

flags.message: method weights differ from the industry default {'dcf_life': 0.6, 'ev_ebitda': 0.25, 'div_yield': 0.15}
flags.justification: div_yield is given zero weight (round-2 C1): the engine's forward DPS metric capitalises the FY2026E peak-earnings dividend, which the report itself calls a timing-and-rate artefact, so it is excluded and the two through-cycle methods renormalise; dcf_life 0.6 / ev_ebitda 0.25 is the house method for a finite-life cyclical and the peak dividend the excluded method prices is the FY2026E payout [S3].

flags.message: konglo lens: price is 1.13x fundamental value (premium); the base case closes 40% of the log gap in 12 months (hsc, ff_deadline); target 6,721 vs fundamental 12-month value 6,215 — explain it in §4 and §6
flags.justification: The konglo lens is the engine's regime step, not a valuation input: the fundamental 12-month value stays at the DCF/multiple blend after the liquidity discount, and the target keeps only the probability-weighted share of the small premium the price carries at the current mark, with the closing share rising with the flags GEMS holds — HSC status with no passive buyer [S9] and a free-float step due by 31 Mar 2027 [S10]. It is explained in §4, §5 and §6 of the report with placeholders, and the overlay parameters are the konglo deck's, not the analyst's.
